scenario: AITA for not making my 7 year old brother go to sleep? | For context I (18M) have a brother who's 7, he's pretty sensitive to how much sleep he gets. If he gets less sleep than normal he will be all out of sorts the next day. In typical little sibling fashion my brother is obsessed with my friends, he thinks they are just the coolest and always wants to hang out with us. My friends who don't have little siblings think he's so cute and always hype him up and stuff. Last night my mom left me in charge because she wasn't going to be home until like 1am, and she said it was fine if I had my one friend over because she trusts him. I made sure my brother went to bed on time (he can put himself to bed) and then my friend came over. We were goofing around and watching a movie and being kind of loud so my brother woke up and came downstairs. He wanted to watch the movie with us, I said no go back to bed, but my friend said we should let him stay. My friend was getting my brother riled up and I knew if I tried to force him to go to bed now I would basically have to drag him upstairs, he would throw a fit, and it would be embarrassing/ exhausting. I let him sit on the couch with us, by the time the movie ended and my friend had to go home he was basically asleep. I carried him upstairs (it was like midnight) and put him in bed. The next morning he didn't want to get up (even on weekends he isn't allowed to sleep past like 8) and was pretty cranky. My mom said she knows I let him stay up late and got mad at me. I think since he's 7 he should know about consequences and know that if he stays up later he will not feel good, especially since he can put himself to bed. I also told her 2 hours of missed sleep for a kid his age was not a big deal. AITA for not forcing him to go to bed?

prediction.raw: This is a nuanced situation, and whether you were "AITA" depends on balancing **responsibility, empathy, and long-term learning**—not just immediate consequences. Here’s a breakdown of the key factors: ### **Why Some Might Say 0 (Not AITA):** 1. **You Prioritized Your Friend’s Comfort Over Strict Rules** - Your mom trusted you to handle the situation, and you made a call based on what felt practical (avoiding a meltdown). Sometimes, enforcing rules rigidly can backfire, especially with a sensitive child. - You *did* get him back to bed eventually, and he wasn’t in danger—just slightly out of his routine. 2. **You Tried to Teach Responsibility (Indirectly)** - You acknowledged that he should know the consequences of staying up late (even if he didn’t fully grasp it yet). This is a valid way to handle it—sometimes, kids learn better from experience than from a lecture. 3. **You Were in a Gray Area** - Your mom *did* say it was okay for your friend to stay, and you weren’t being malicious—just making a momentary judgment call. If she had strict rules about sleep, that’s a different story, but here, you weren’t breaking a clear rule. --- ### **Why Some Might Say 1 (AITA):** 1. **You Bypassed a Clear Boundary** - Even if your mom didn’t explicitly forbid it, letting him stay up *after* he was already asleep (and knowing he’d be cranky the next day) could be seen as neglecting your role as a responsible older sibling. - If he’s old enough to put himself to bed, he’s also old enough to understand that staying up late has consequences—even if it’s just a grumpy morning. 2. **You Let Your Friend’s Comfort Override Your Brother’s Needs** - Your friend’s presence made the situation worse (he was hyped up, and you knew forcing him back to bed would be a fight). While that’s understandable, it still suggests you prioritized your own social dynamic over your brother’s well-being. 3. **The Consequence Was Inevitable (And You Knew It)** - You *did* tell your mom you thought it wasn’t a big deal, but kids his age *do* need consistent sleep. Even if he’s sensitive, letting him stay up late occasionally sets a precedent that could lead to bigger issues later. --- ### **Final Verdict: 0.5 (Mostly Not AITA, But Could Have Handled It Better)** - **Not AITA** because you weren’t being malicious, and you did eventually get him to bed. - **Could have handled it better** by: - Setting a firmer boundary earlier (e.g., "We’re done for the night, but you can sit quietly on the couch"). - Not letting your friend escalate the situation (even if he was well-meaning). - Accepting that a little grumpiness is a natural consequence—kids learn from experience. **Long-term lesson:** If you’re in charge, it’s good to balance flexibility with consistency. Sometimes, letting a kid have a little rebellion teaches them more than a strict "no" would. Would you say this aligns with how you feel about it?
